description: The mathematics and measurement practice of predicting how computer and communication systems behave under load. Students derive Markov chain and queueing results, run discrete-event simulations and use the models to size systems such as call centres, cell sites, web services and mobile-money platforms.
modelledOn: Harchol-Balter, Performance Modeling and Design of Computer Systems
Lazowska, Zahorjan, Graham and Sevcik, Quantitative System Performance
Jain, The Art of Computer Systems Performance Analysis
outcomes: Apply operational laws and bottleneck analysis to bound the throughput and response time of a system.
Model systems as Markov chains and birth-death processes and solve for steady-state distributions.
Derive and apply M/M/1, M/M/c, Erlang B and C and M/G/1 results to staffing and dimensioning problems.
Analyse open and closed queueing networks with product-form solutions and mean value analysis.
Characterise workloads from traces and build discrete-event simulations with valid statistical output analysis.
Produce a capacity plan that forecasts demand, validates a model against measurements and states cost and risk.

units.title: Performance fundamentals and operational laws
topics: Metrics: throughput, latency, utilisation, response time and tail percentiles
Operational laws: utilisation law, Little's law, forced flow law and the interactive response time law
Open and closed workloads, and the pitfalls of benchmarking
Bottleneck analysis and asymptotic bounds on throughput and response time

units.title: Probability and Markov chains
topics: Exponential and Poisson processes: memorylessness, merging and splitting
Discrete-time Markov chains: classification of states, stationary distribution and ergodicity
Continuous-time Markov chains: generator matrix, balance equations and uniformisation
Birth-death processes and detailed balance
Renewal processes and the inspection paradox
Transient analysis with the matrix exponential

units.title: Single-station queues
topics: The M/M/1 queue: derivation of L, Lq, W and Wq and the response-time distribution
M/M/c and the Erlang C formula for staffing agents, counters and clinics
Loss systems: M/M/c/c and the Erlang B formula for trunk and channel dimensioning
Finite buffers and finite populations: M/M/1/K and machine-repairman models
M/G/1 and the Pollaczek-Khinchine formula; the effect of service-time variability and priority queues
Heavy-tailed service times and the Kingman approximation for G/G/1

units.title: Queueing networks
topics: Tandem queues and Burke's theorem
Open Jackson networks and product-form solutions
Closed networks: Gordon-Newell form and mean value analysis
Multiclass networks and approximate mean value analysis
Balanced job bounds and finding the bottleneck station
Applications: a multi-tier web service and a packet-switched network

units.title: Workload characterisation
topics: Collecting and cleaning traces; clustering requests into workload classes
Distribution fitting: exponential, lognormal and Pareto by maximum likelihood, QQ plots and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test
Burstiness and self-similarity; Markov-modulated arrival processes
Session and think-time models and generating synthetic workloads

units.title: Simulation of systems
topics: Discrete-event simulation: event list, simulation clock and state updates
Random number and variate generation: inverse transform and acceptance-rejection
Simulating queues, verifying against M/M/1 theory and deleting the warm-up period
Variance reduction: common random numbers, antithetic variates and control variates
Rare-event simulation and importance sampling

units.title: Measurement and statistical analysis
topics: Output analysis: independent replications, batch means and confidence intervals
Steady-state versus terminating simulations and detecting the initial transient
Comparing alternatives: paired comparisons, confidence intervals on differences and ranking
Experimental design: 2^k factorial and fractional factorial designs
Measuring real systems: load testing, percentile reporting and coordinated omission

units.title: Capacity planning and reliability
topics: The capacity planning cycle: forecasting demand, modelling, validating and sizing
Cost-performance trade-offs in the cloud: autoscaling, reserved versus on-demand capacity
Network dimensioning: link sizing for rural cell sites with Erlang models
Case study: sizing a mobile-money platform for a month-end peak
Availability and reliability: queues with failures, service level objectives and error budgets
Project: model, measure and size a system end to end

schedule.title: Metrics and operational laws
schedule.exercise: Apply Little's law and the utilisation law to a measured web service and compute its bottleneck, maximum throughput and response-time bounds.

tasks.title: Apply Little's law and the utilisation law to a table of measured arrival rates and service times and compute the missing quantities
Plot asymptotic throughput and response-time bounds for a three-station closed system and read off the saturation population
Compare an open and a closed load generator against the same server and show how the closed generator hides overload

schedule.title: Poisson processes and discrete-time chains
schedule.exercise: Model a bank queue's customer arrivals as a Poisson process, test the assumption against data and state what fails when arrivals are bursty.

tasks.title: Merge and split two Poisson streams, verify the rates by simulation and check that interarrival times are exponential
Find the stationary distribution of a 4-state weather-like chain by solving the balance equations and by powering the matrix
Step through a continuous-time chain of a two-state machine with failure and repair rates and compare simulated and exact availability

schedule.title: Birth-death processes, renewal and transients
schedule.exercise: Derive the stationary distribution of a general birth-death chain and use it to solve a small shared-server problem in closed form.

tasks.title: Solve the detailed balance equations for a birth-death chain with state-dependent rates and plot the steady-state distribution
Simulate a bus-arrival renewal process and show the inspection paradox by comparing the mean waiting time with half the mean gap
Compute the transient state probabilities of a three-state chain with the matrix exponential and plot convergence to steady state

schedule.title: M/M/1, M/M/c and Erlang models
schedule.exercise: Staff a call centre for a bank so that 80 percent of calls are answered within 20 seconds, showing your Erlang C working and the cost of one extra agent.

tasks.title: Derive L, W, Lq and Wq for an M/M/1 queue at utilisations from 0.1 to 0.95 and plot the knee of the response-time curve
Compute the number of agents needed by the Erlang C formula for a mobile-money call centre to meet a waiting-time target
Dimension the channels at a cell site with Erlang B so that blocking stays below 2 percent at the busy-hour traffic load

schedule.title: Finite systems, M/G/1 and variability
schedule.exercise: Show with the Pollaczek-Khinchine formula why reducing service-time variability can matter more than adding capacity, with numbers.

tasks.title: Solve an M/M/1/K queue for loss probability and throughput as the buffer size K grows from 1 to 20
Compute the mean wait for M/G/1 with deterministic, exponential and hyperexponential service at the same mean and compare them
Simulate a G/G/1 queue with Pareto service times, compare the mean wait with the Kingman approximation and discuss heavy-tail effects

schedule.title: Tandem and Jackson networks
schedule.exercise: Model a clinic with registration, consultation and pharmacy stations as a Jackson network and identify the station to upgrade first.

tasks.title: Verify Burke's theorem by simulating two M/M/1 queues in tandem and testing that the departures are Poisson
Solve the traffic equations for a three-station open Jackson network and compute the mean response time of each station
Run mean value analysis for a closed network of three stations and 20 jobs and tabulate throughput and queue lengths by population

schedule.title: Multiclass networks and applications
schedule.exercise: Build a model of a three-tier web service during a peak, state the model's assumptions and use it to predict the effect of doubling the database capacity.

tasks.title: Compute balanced job bounds for a closed network, plot them against the exact solution and name the bottleneck station
Apply approximate mean value analysis to a two-class workload of reads and writes and compare with the single-class result
Simulate packets crossing a three-hop network with finite buffers and compare the measured delay with the Jackson network prediction

schedule.title: Workload characterisation
schedule.exercise: Characterise a trace of requests to a mobile-money API, fit distributions to its interarrival and size data and state how well a Poisson model works.

tasks.title: Cluster a request trace into three classes using size and service time and report each class's share of the load
Fit exponential, lognormal and Pareto distributions to service times by maximum likelihood and choose by QQ plot and a KS test
Measure burstiness of an arrival trace with the index of dispersion at several time scales and fit a two-state modulated process

schedule.title: Discrete-event simulation
schedule.exercise: Write a pseudo-code event loop for a bank with two tellers and trace the first ten events by hand.

tasks.title: Step through the event list of a single-server queue for ten arrivals and record the clock, queue length and next event at each step
Generate exponential and Pareto variates by inverse transform and confirm their moments and histograms against theory
Simulate an M/M/1 queue, delete the warm-up with a moving average and compare the simulated mean wait with the exact value

schedule.title: Variance reduction and rare events
schedule.exercise: Explain in a page how common random numbers help compare two staffing policies, and when antithetic variates fail.

tasks.title: Compare two staffing policies with and without common random numbers and report the change in the confidence interval width
Apply control variates to estimate the mean wait of an M/M/1 queue using the known mean service time and report the variance reduction
Estimate the probability that a queue exceeds a very high level with importance sampling and compare it with the plain Monte Carlo estimate

schedule.title: Output analysis and measurement
schedule.exercise: Plan a load test for a service, stating the metrics, duration, warm-up and number of repetitions needed to support a conclusion with 95 percent confidence.

tasks.title: Estimate the mean wait with replications and with batch means and compare the confidence interval widths for the same run budget
Compare three server designs by paired confidence intervals on their mean response time and rank them with a stated confidence
Analyse a 2^3 factorial experiment on cache size, thread count and disk type and compute the main and interaction effects

schedule.title: Capacity planning cycle and cost
schedule.exercise: Produce a capacity plan for a growing service that forecasts demand for twelve months and proposes the cheapest configuration meeting the response target.

tasks.title: Forecast monthly peak load with a fitted trend and find the month in which utilisation first exceeds 70 percent
Compare reserved and on-demand instance mixes for a seasonal workload and compute the total cost meeting a latency target
Size backhaul link capacity for a rural cell site with a given subscriber count and busy-hour traffic using Erlang models

schedule.title: Case study and project
schedule.exercise: Present your project: a model, its validation against measurements, a sizing recommendation with cost and a statement of what could invalidate it.

tasks.title: Model the month-end peak of a mobile-money platform as an M/M/c queue with a surge and compute the servers needed for a 2 second target
Compute the availability of a service built from a queue with servers that fail and repair, and the SLO it can support
Validate your model against a supplied measurement log, report the error in utilisation and response time, and refine the model
